WITH latest AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (file_hash, detector_version)
         file_hash, content_type, detector_version, checked_at, outcome, confidence
  FROM detection_checks
  WHERE outcome <> 'error'
  ORDER BY file_hash, detector_version, checked_at DESC, check_id DESC
)
SELECT date_trunc('week', checked_at)::date                                          AS week_start,
       content_type,
       detector_version,
       COUNT(*)                                                                      AS files,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE confidence <> 'low' AND outcome = 'watermarked')       AS watermarked,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE confidence <> 'low' AND outcome = 'partial')           AS partial,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE confidence <> 'low' AND outcome = 'not_watermarked')   AS not_watermarked,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE confidence = 'low')                                    AS low_confidence,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE confidence <> 'low' AND outcome IN ('watermarked', 'partial'))::numeric
             / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE confidence <> 'low'), 0), 3)            AS watermarked_share
FROM latest
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3;

Explanation. The unit of the report is a file per detector version, not a check. DISTINCT ON (file_hash, detector_version) keeps the first row of each key in the ORDER BY, so ordering by checked_at DESC, check_id DESC keeps the latest check, with the greater id winning a tie at the same second (Very Hard). Error checks are removed in the WHERE, before DISTINCT ON chooses: filtering them afterwards would let an error hide the result before it and drop the file. The week comes from the chosen check, so a file re-checked across the week boundary counts once, in the later week. Low-confidence results go only into low_confidence; the three outcome columns and the share use the other files. NULLIF turns a group with no confident file into a NULL share instead of a division error, and the ::numeric cast keeps the division exact before ROUND.

Complexity. One sort by (file, version, time) for DISTINCT ON and a hash aggregate: O(n log n) for n checks. In production keep a "latest result per (file, version)" table updated by upsert as checks arrive (only a later checked_at, or an equal one with a greater id, replaces a row) and aggregate weekly from it.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake and BigQuery: no DISTINCT ON; use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY file_hash, detector_version ORDER BY checked_at DESC, check_id DESC) = 1; COUNT_IF / COUNTIF for the filtered counts; DIV0NULL (Snowflake) or SAFE_DIVIDE (BigQuery) for the share; BigQuery's DATE_TRUNC(…, WEEK) starts on Sunday, so use WEEK(MONDAY). Spark SQL: ROW_NUMBER in a subquery (or max_by(struct, …)), count_if, date_trunc('week', …) starts on Monday. MySQL 8: ROW_NUMBER in a derived table, SUM(CASE …), and NULLIF for the share.

Edge cases built into the data. Files checked once and several times; a file whose latest check is low confidence after a high-confidence one; files checked by both versions and by one; groups with only some outcomes. Hard: a second week; an error check after a valid result (must not replace it); a file with only error checks (no result); a file re-checked in the next week. Very Hard: two checks of one file at the same second with different outcomes (the greater id wins); checks at 23:59:59 on Sunday and 00:00:00 on Monday; a pre-release detector version whose only results are low confidence (share NULL).

Common mistakes. Counting checks instead of files; MAX(checked_at) with a join back, which returns two rows on a tie; MAX(check_id) as "latest"; filtering errors after choosing the latest check; collapsing across detector versions; putting low-confidence results in the outcome counts or the denominator; integer division (a share of 0 or 1); grouping by the week of the first check.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A file's cross-version result needs a rule (the newest version that checked it, or the newest generally available version); adding the per-version rows double counts files checked by both. (2) Join each file's latest result under the old and the new version on file_hash, and count agreement and each kind of disagreement per content type and confidence level; only hashes and outcomes are needed, never content. (3) Upsert the latest-per-key table, then recompute only the weeks whose rows changed: a re-check moves a file out of one week and into another, so both weeks are recomputed. (4) Publish counts above a minimum group size and suppress or coarsen smaller cells; per-day numbers for a rare content type may point at individual files or requesters.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape, but counts checks, lets errors replace results, or mixes low confidence into the outcomes. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains the filter-before-choose order and the tie-break, and gives sound answers on version disagreement and small groups.

Strong signals. Asks what the unit is (file, check, or file per version) before writing SQL; checks that watermarked + partial + not_watermarked + low_confidence = files. Red flags. Reports a share for a group with no confident results as 0; keeps or asks for file contents to "verify" outcomes.

WITH scored AS (                        -- one row per residue with a score
  SELECT DISTINCT prediction_id, residue_index, plddt
  FROM residue_confidence
  WHERE plddt IS NOT NULL
), per_prediction AS (
  SELECT p.release, p.organism, p.prediction_id,
         COUNT(*)                                             AS residues,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE s.plddt >= 90)                AS very_high,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE s.plddt >= 70 AND s.plddt < 90) AS confident,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE s.plddt >= 50 AND s.plddt < 70) AS low,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE s.plddt < 50)                 AS very_low
  FROM predictions p
  JOIN scored s ON s.prediction_id = p.prediction_id
  WHERE NOT p.withdrawn
  GROUP BY p.release, p.organism, p.prediction_id
)
SELECT release,
       organism,
       COUNT(*)                                          AS predictions,
       SUM(residues)                                     AS residues,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(very_high) / SUM(residues), 1)  AS very_high_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(confident) / SUM(residues), 1)  AS confident_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(low) / SUM(residues), 1)        AS low_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(very_low) / SUM(residues), 1)   AS very_low_pct,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE 2 * very_low > residues)   AS mostly_very_low
FROM per_prediction
GROUP BY release, organism
ORDER BY release, organism;

Explanation. Clean the residues first: drop unscored ones and count each (prediction, residue) once (Very Hard). Then aggregate twice. The per-prediction level gives each prediction's band counts, which "mostly very low" needs (2 × very_low > residues is "strictly more than half" in integers). The per-organism level sums residue counts and divides, which makes the percentages residue-weighted: a 1 000-residue prediction weighs a hundred times a 10-residue one, as it should when the question is "what share of this organism's residues is confident". Each band includes its lower edge, so 90.00, 70.00 and 50.00 fall in the higher band. Withdrawn predictions (Hard) are excluded before anything is counted; each release is grouped on its own.

Complexity. One pass over the residues with a distinct (a hash or sort on three columns), a hash aggregate per prediction, and a small one per organism: O(r) to O(r log r) for r residue rows. At release scale the per-prediction band counts are computed once when the confidence files are written and stored with the prediction, so this check reads one row per prediction.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake: COUNT_IF, IFF; DIV0 for safe division. BigQuery: COUNTIF, SAFE_DIVIDE, ROUND(x, 1); NUMERIC keeps exact edges, FLOAT64 would put 90.00 at risk only if it were computed rather than stored. Spark SQL: count_if or SUM(CASE …), DECIMAL(5,2) for exact edges. MySQL 8: SUM(CASE …) instead of FILTER, DECIMAL(5,2), and ROUND behaves the same on exact decimals.

Edge cases built into the data. Residues at exactly 90.00, 89.99, 70.00, 69.99, 50.00 and 49.99 in one prediction; a prediction mostly in the lowest band; organisms with predictions of different lengths, so weighted and unweighted shares differ. Hard: a second release with an organism new in it; an accession predicted in both releases with different confidence; a withdrawn prediction; a prediction with exactly half its residues below 50. Very Hard: unscored residues in several predictions; a prediction that is exactly half very low among scored residues but more than half if NULLs count as very low; residue rows delivered twice, one set of which would make a prediction look mostly very low.

Common mistakes. > instead of >= on the edges; averaging per-prediction percentages; >= 0.5 for "mostly"; counting withdrawn predictions; COUNT(*) including NULL scores, or ELSE 'very_low' that sweeps NULLs into the lowest band; no de-duplication; rounding per prediction and then averaging; integer division.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Fragments overlap: either report per fragment (and say so), or map fragment residues to the full-length sequence and count each sequence position once, choosing which fragment's score to keep (for example the one where the position is furthest from a fragment end) and stating the rule. (2) Store band edges as versioned configuration with the release that used them, compute each release's report with its own edges, and recompute old releases under new edges only as a labelled comparison. (3) Compute per-prediction band counts when the confidence file is written, store them as columns, and aggregate per organism from those: a scan of one row per prediction instead of per residue. (4) Store the per-residue scores in a compact array per prediction (or a small binary file next to the structure file), served from the same release snapshot as the bulk archive, with a checksum both use.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape, but band edges, weighting or the "mostly" rule are wrong. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also handles fragments and versioned band edges with clear rules, and moves the per-residue work to write time.

Strong signals. Asks whether the edges are inclusive and whether shares are residue-weighted before writing SQL; keeps the work to data quality and says nothing about what a low score means biologically. Red flags. Treats a NULL score as zero confidence; draws a medical or functional conclusion from a confidence band.

WITH counted AS (
  SELECT run_id, project, config_hash, code_version, data_snapshot, seed, started_at, final_metric
  FROM runs
  WHERE status = 'completed'
    AND final_metric IS NOT NULL
    AND seed IS NOT NULL
), ranked AS (
  SELECT project, started_at, final_metric,
         ROW_NUMBER()  OVER w AS rn,
         FIRST_VALUE(final_metric) OVER w AS first_metric
  FROM counted
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY project, config_hash, code_version, data_snapshot, seed
               ORDER BY started_at, run_id)
), rerun_diffs AS (
  SELECT project,
         date_trunc('month', started_at)::date AS month,
         ABS(final_metric - first_metric)      AS diff
  FROM ranked
  WHERE rn > 1
)
SELECT month,
       project,
       COUNT(*)                                           AS reruns,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE diff > {{tolerance}})       AS not_reproduced,
       MAX(diff)                                          AS max_abs_diff
FROM rerun_diffs
GROUP BY month, project
ORDER BY month, project;

Explanation. Filter first: only completed runs with a metric can be a first run or a rerun, so a failed first attempt (every level) or a cancelled run that carries a metric (Very Hard) never becomes the baseline. Runs without a seed are excluded explicitly: PARTITION BY and GROUP BY treat NULLs as equal, so two seedless runs would otherwise look like a recipe and its rerun (Very Hard). The window orders each recipe by started_at, run_id, so a tie in the same minute goes to the smaller id; FIRST_VALUE is the baseline every rerun is compared with (not the previous run, which lets slow drift hide). The difference is NUMERIC, so "strictly greater than the tolerance" is exact, and a difference equal to it reproduced. The month is the rerun's own.

Complexity. One window sort over the counted runs, partitioned by recipe, and a hash aggregate: O(n log n). Incrementally, keep a per-recipe baseline table (first run id and metric), insert-only except when a run that started earlier finishes later, and append rerun rows with their difference as runs complete.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake: QUALIFY can filter rn > 1; FIRST_VALUE the same; DATE_TRUNC('month', …); COUNT_IF. BigQuery: named WINDOW clauses work; NUMERIC for exact metrics; COUNTIF. Spark SQL: first(final_metric) OVER w (make sure the frame starts at the partition start, the default with ORDER BY), DECIMAL(8,4). MySQL 8: named windows are supported; no FILTER, so SUM(diff > tol); DECIMAL(8,4) keeps exactness. In every engine, a NULL in a partition key forms its own group, so the explicit seed IS NOT NULL is needed everywhere.

Edge cases built into the data. A recipe whose first attempt failed and whose last attempt failed; a rerun exactly the tolerance away (reproduced) and one well outside it; recipes with up to four runs, so comparing with the previous run differs from comparing with the first. Hard: a second month; a first run late in September with its rerun in October (reported in October); runs that differ only in seed, and only in data snapshot (different recipes). Very Hard: two runs of a recipe started in the same minute (the smaller id is the first); two runs with no seed and otherwise identical recipes (not a rerun); a cancelled run carrying a metric before the first completed run (ignored).

Common mistakes. LAG instead of the first run; >= for the tolerance; filtering status after ranking, so a failed run is the baseline; leaving seed (or snapshot) out of the key; grouping NULL seeds; MIN(started_at) with a join back that returns two rows on a tie; reporting a rerun in its recipe's first month; casting metrics to float.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A per-project (or per-metric) tolerance table joined on project, with an owner and a review date, and the report shows each project's tolerance next to its count, so a very wide one is visible rather than hidden. (2) Record environment fields (accelerator type, library versions, container digest, number of devices) and report reruns whose recipes match but environments differ separately from fully identical reruns; a difference there points at the environment, not the code. (3) With many reruns, compare with the recipe's median, or report the spread (range or standard deviation) per recipe, and flag recipes whose spread exceeds the tolerance; say that "first run" makes the baseline an accident of order. (4) Maintain the baseline per recipe on completion; a run that started earlier but finished later can replace the baseline, which changes earlier rows: recompute that recipe only.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape, but compares with the previous run, includes failed runs, or misses part of the recipe. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains the NULL-key trap and the tie-break, and proposes credible per-project tolerances and environment diagnostics.

Strong signals. Asks what makes two runs "the same recipe" and what to do with a missing seed before writing SQL; treats non-reproduction as a signal to investigate, not a verdict. Red flags. Claims any real model or result is non-reproducible; compares floats with =.

def pareto_front(runs):
    if any(hours < 0 for _, hours, _ in runs):
        return None
    last = {}
    for run_id, hours, score in runs:          # the last record of a run wins
        last[run_id] = (hours, score)
    items = sorted((hours, -score, run_id) for run_id, (hours, score) in last.items() if score is not None)
    out = []
    best = None                                # best score among strictly cheaper runs
    i, n = 0, len(items)
    while i < n:
        hours, neg_top = items[i][0], items[i][1]
        j = i
        while j < n and items[j][0] == hours and items[j][1] == neg_top:
            j += 1                             # runs equal to the group's top: an equal set
        if best is None or -neg_top > best:
            out.extend(items[k][2] for k in range(i, j))
            best = -neg_top
        while j < n and items[j][0] == hours:  # the rest of this hours group is beaten by its top
            j += 1
        i = j
    return out

Explanation. Sort by hours ascending, score descending, id ascending. A run can only be beaten by a run with no more hours, so after the sort every possible beater of a run is before it or in its own hours group. Within an hours group only the top score can survive (the others are beaten by it), and every run equal to that top survives together, since equal runs do not beat each other. The top survives exactly when its score is strictly above the best score of all cheaper runs: a cheaper run with an equal or higher score beats it. The running best is that maximum, and it only changes when a group survives (a group that does not survive has a top no higher than best). Output comes out in hours order and, within an equal set, in id order, as required. At Hard, unscored runs are dropped before the sort and a negative hours value anywhere returns None; at Very Hard the dictionary keeps each run's last record, including a last record without a score.

Complexity. O(n log n) for the sort and O(n) for the scan, O(n) memory. The timing test (80 000 runs, about 85% of them on the front) runs in about 0.2–0.3 s in CPython, and generating its data takes about 0.1 s.

The middle approach. The most likely middle solution keeps the current front as a list and, for each run, checks it against every member (and removes the members it beats). That is O(n·f) for a front of size f. The timing data is built so the front is large (scores rise with hours plus small noise), so it does about n·f/2 ≈ 3 × 10⁹ comparisons; when timed for this template, 10 000 runs of the same data already took 5.3 s in CPython and the full 80 000 would take several minutes, so it fails the 8 s limit clearly. Comparing every pair (O(n²)) is worse. Sorting by score descending and keeping the least hours seen so far is the mirror of the reference and passes; a balanced tree or bisect over the front for an online version also passes.

Dialect notes. In Java sort an array of records with a comparator on (hours, −score, id), or use TreeMap for the online variant. In SQL the front is a window query: a run is on it when its score is strictly above MAX(score) OVER (ORDER BY hours RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) and equal to the maximum score in its own hours group. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. No runs ([]); one run; same hours with a higher score; same score with fewer hours; a staircase where every run is on the front; one run beating all others; more hours for the same score; output order by hours rather than input, score or id. Hard: equal pairs kept in id order; unscored runs; no scored run at all ([]); zero hours; negative hours (None). Very Hard: a run re-logged with a better score, a worse one, no score, and a score after none; a re-logged run that becomes equal to another.

Common mistakes. Using strict < and > together, which keeps runs that a same-hours run with a higher score beats; dropping one of an equal pair; ordering the output by score or input order; not handling a group whose top equals the best so far (it is beaten); taking the first record of a re-logged run; raising on bad input instead of returning None.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Induction over the sorted order: the invariant is that best equals the best score among strictly cheaper runs, and the survival test is exactly "no cheaper run with an equal or higher score, and no same-hours run with a higher score". (2) With three objectives the front is no longer a staircase; sort by one objective and keep a 2D structure (a Fenwick or segment tree over a compressed second objective storing the best third) for O(n log² n) or a divide-and-conquer skyline; at 80 000 runs either is fine. (3) Keep the front in a sorted container keyed by hours; a new run is rejected if the predecessor's score is at least its own, otherwise inserted and its dominated successors (a contiguous range) removed, amortised O(log f). (4) An additive or multiplicative epsilon on the score (say within 1% of the best score available at that cost or less); compute it with the same scan by comparing against best × 0.99.

Rubric anchors. 2: an O(n·f) or O(n²) version, or the right idea with wrong ties. 3: all tests pass in O(n log n). 4: also proves the scan and handles the three-objective and online follow-ups well.

Strong signals. Asks how equal runs and same-hours runs are treated before coding; tests with a staircase and an equal pair. Red flags. Combines hours and score into one weighted number and sorts by it (that is a different question); assumes ids are unique when the statement says they may not be.

def allocate_hours(requests, budget, prefer="id"):
    if budget < 0 or any(hours < 0 for _, hours in requests):
        return None
    total = {}
    for project, hours in requests:            # repeated projects add up, first position kept
        total[project] = total.get(project, 0) + hours
    projects = list(total)
    alloc = {}
    left = budget
    todo = sorted(projects, key=lambda p: total[p])
    k, n = 0, len(todo)
    # A request at most an equal share of what is left (r <= left // (n - k)) is met in full.
    while k < n and total[todo[k]] * (n - k) <= left:
        alloc[todo[k]] = total[todo[k]]
        left -= total[todo[k]]
        k += 1
    rest = todo[k:]
    if rest:                                   # every remaining request is above the level
        level, spare = divmod(left, len(rest))
        for p in rest:
            alloc[p] = level
        key = (lambda p: (total[p], p)) if prefer == "smaller" else None
        for p in sorted(rest, key=key)[:spare]:
            alloc[p] += 1
    return [(p, alloc[p]) for p in projects]

Explanation. Sort by request and walk upwards with the budget still to share (left) and the number of projects still to serve (n − k). If the smallest remaining request is at most an equal share of what is left, every remaining project could get at least that much, so the level is at least this request and it is met in full. The first time a request is above the equal share, every remaining request is too (they are sorted), so all of them get the level L = left // (n − k) and left % (n − k) hours are spare, fewer than the uncapped projects. That L is the largest level that fits: everyone capped so far is at or below it, and one more hour for each uncapped project would exceed the budget. The comparison is done as r × (n − k) <= left in integers, so no float can give a project an extra hour. Spare hours go to the uncapped projects in the prefer order. When the budget covers every request, the walk caps everyone and leaves the rest unallocated. Input order is restored from the dictionary, which keeps first-appearance order; at Very Hard it also adds up repeated projects.

Complexity. O(n log n) for the sorts, O(n) memory, and the arithmetic is exact for any budget. The timing test (50 000 staggered requests, a budget of about 7.9 × 10⁹ hours, about 90% of the projects capped) runs in about 0.15 s in CPython, plus about 0.07 s to generate.

The middle approach. Handing out one hour at a time (or a round-robin loop over projects) is O(budget): about 8 × 10⁹ steps here, hopeless. The likely middle solution is "rounds of equal shares". There are two common versions, and they behave very differently. (a) Each round finds the single smallest remaining request with min(), caps it if it fits the current equal share, removes it with list.remove, and recomputes the share: one project per round, so O(n²) when most projects are capped, which the staggered requests ensure. When timed for this template, 20 000 projects took 22 s in CPython, and the full 50 000 would take over two minutes, so it fails the 8 s limit clearly. (b) Each round gives every remaining project min(share, need) at once, so all projects at or below the share are capped together, and repeats until the share is zero, then hands out the spare hours by the tie rule. def allocate_hours(requests, budget, prefer="id"):
    if budget < 0 or any(hours < 0 for _, hours in requests):
        return None
    total = {}
    for project, hours in requests:            # repeated projects add up, first position kept
        total[project] = total.get(project, 0) + hours
    projects = list(total)
    alloc = {}
    left = budget
    todo = sorted(projects, key=lambda p: total[p])
    k, n = 0, len(todo)
    # A request at most an equal share of what is left (r <= left // (n - k)) is met in full.
    while k < n and total[todo[k]] * (n - k) <= left:
        alloc[todo[k]] = total[todo[k]]
        left -= total[todo[k]]
        k += 1
    rest = todo[k:]
    if rest:                                   # every remaining request is above the level
        level, spare = divmod(left, len(rest))
        for p in rest:
            alloc[p] = level
        key = (lambda p: (total[p], p)) if prefer == "smaller" else None
        for p in sorted(rest, key=key)[:spare]:
            alloc[p] += 1
    return [(p, alloc[p]) for p in projects]

def residue_contacts(residues, cutoff, min_conf=0):
    # Cell list: bucket residues into cubes of side `cutoff`. Two residues within the
    # cutoff are in the same cube or in neighbouring cubes (26 around each), so each
    # cube is compared with itself and with 13 of its neighbours (each pair once).
    c = cutoff
    c2 = c * c
    grid = {}
    for res in residues:
        if res[4] >= min_conf:
            key = (res[1] // c, res[2] // c, res[3] // c)       # floor division, negatives too
            cell = grid.get(key)
            if cell is None:
                grid[key] = [res]
            else:
                cell.append(res)
    forward = [(dx, dy, dz) for dx in (-1, 0, 1) for dy in (-1, 0, 1) for dz in (-1, 0, 1)
               if (dx, dy, dz) > (0, 0, 0)]                     # 13 of the 26 neighbours
    out = []

    def check(a, b):
        ex, ey, ez = b[1] - a[1], b[2] - a[2], b[3] - a[3]
        if ex * ex + ey * ey + ez * ez <= c2:                   # exact, integers
            na, nb = a[0], b[0]
            if nb - na >= 3:
                out.append((na, nb))
            elif na - nb >= 3:
                out.append((nb, na))

    for (gx, gy, gz), cell in grid.items():
        m = len(cell)
        for i in range(m):
            for j in range(i + 1, m):
                check(cell[i], cell[j])
        for dx, dy, dz in forward:
            other = grid.get((gx + dx, gy + dy, gz + dz))
            if other is not None:
                for a in cell:
                    for b in other:
                        check(a, b)
    out.sort()
    return out

Explanation. Two atoms within the cutoff differ by at most one cutoff along every axis, so if space is cut into cubes of side cutoff, a residue's partners can only be in its own cube or in one of the 26 cubes around it. Bucketing every counted residue by (x // cutoff, y // cutoff, z // cutoff) in a dict takes one pass; then each cube is compared with itself (pairs i < j) and with 13 of its neighbours, one from each opposite pair (the offsets greater than (0, 0, 0) in tuple order), so each pair of residues is examined exactly once. The distance test is exact: squared integer distances against cutoff * cutoff, inclusive. The separation rule is applied to residue numbers, and the pair is written smaller number first, because cube order says nothing about residue order. Residues below min_conf never enter the grid, which removes them and every contact they were part of. Python's // floors negative coordinates, so a residue at x = -1 lands in cube -1, next to cube 0; truncation toward zero (int(x / cutoff)) would merge cubes -1 and 0 into one double-width cube, which is still correct but slower, so it is not a bug here, only worth a question.

Complexity. O(n) to bucket and O(n · m) pair checks, where m is the number of residues in 14 cubes around a residue, so O(n + contacts) at protein-like densities; the final sort is O(c log c) for c contacts. The timing test (50 000 residues in a box about 37 cutoffs wide, about one residue per cube volume, about 86 000 to 100 000 contacts) takes about 0.6 to 0.7 s in CPython, and generating the input about 0.1 s. Visiting all 27 cubes and keeping only b - a >= 3 (each pair seen from both sides) takes about 1.05 s and passes. Comparing every pair took 5.3 s at 6 000 residues; at 50 000 that is about 370 s, extrapolated, some 500 times the reference.

The middle approach. The likely middle answer sorts residues by x and, for each one, scans forward while the x difference is at most the cutoff, checking the full distance only for those. On an extended chain lying along x that is fast. On a compact fold it is not: each slab one cutoff wide holds about n · cutoff / side residues, about 1 300 here, so the scan is O(n² · cutoff / side), roughly n^(5/3) for a globule. Measured on the timing test it takes about 15 to 19 s (23 to 31 times the reference), well over the 8 s limit. A k-d tree (for example scipy.spatial.cKDTree.query_pairs, where SciPy is available) is another correct sublinear method and acceptable if the candidate handles the inclusive boundary (query with a radius a hair above the cutoff and filter with the exact integer test) and the separation rule; ask what it costs to build. Sorting by a space-filling curve and scanning a window is not exact without extra checks.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++, pack the three cube coordinates into one 64-bit key for a hash map, or sort residues by cube key and binary-search neighbours; the squared distance fits in a 64-bit integer for coordinates below about 10⁹. NumPy can vectorise the per-cube-pair comparisons with broadcasting. In SQL, add integer cube columns and self-join on b.cx BETWEEN a.cx - 1 AND a.cx + 1 (and the same for cy, cz) with b.residue_number - a.residue_number >= 3 and the squared-distance test; PostGIS offers ST_3DDWithin with a spatial index. In Spark, emit each residue to its own cube and to the 13 forward neighbours, then join by cube key. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A pair exactly at the cutoff, along an axis and on a 3-4-5 triangle (contact); one thousandth beyond the cutoff (not a contact); sequence separations of 1, 2 and 3; negative coordinates and a contact across zero; a contact across a cube corner, diagonal in all three axes (missed by anyone who checks only the 6 face neighbours); an extended strand with no contacts ([]). Hard adds a residue exactly at the confidence floor (counted) and one point below (left out), and a low-confidence residue whose contacts all disappear. Very Hard adds residue numbers out of list order, where separation is by number, and a numbering gap that makes list neighbours into contacts.

Common mistakes. math.dist or sqrt compared with the cutoff, which can misjudge the exact boundary; < cutoff instead of <=; separation by list position instead of residue number; pairs reported twice or as (b, a); checking only face neighbours; cube side smaller than the cutoff with only one ring of neighbours; filtering low-confidence residues after finding contacts but forgetting one side of the pair; sorting the output by cube order instead of residue numbers.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Each entry is independent, so the job parallelises by entry; at an 8 Å cutoff a folded protein has a few to about ten contacts per residue, so the output is several times the residue count in pairs, best stored as two integer arrays per entry, compressed. (2) Bucket with the largest cutoff once and store the squared distance with each pair; smaller cutoffs are then a filter. Cubes of the smallest cutoff with a wider neighbourhood also work. (3) Diff the two sorted pair lists per entry; report added and removed contacts with the confidence of both residues, and say plainly that a contact between low-confidence residues is weakly supported by the prediction. Geometry only, no biological claim. (4) Residue identity becomes (chain, number); the separation rule applies only within a chain (every inter-chain pair is eligible), and the output names both chains.

Rubric anchors. 2: all pairs, or a slab scan presented as fast, or a float distance with a wrong boundary. 3: all tests pass with a cell list (or a k-d tree with the exact boundary), separation by residue number, confidence floor handled. 4: also explains why the slab scan is still quadratic on a compact fold, why the cube side must be at least the cutoff, why 13 neighbours suffice, and answers the several-cutoffs and version-diff follow-ups concretely.

Strong signals. Asks whether the boundary is inclusive and whether coordinates can be negative before coding; estimates the number of residues per cube. Red flags. "Distances are floats, so compare with a small epsilon"; reporting contacts between bonded neighbours.

def ablation_pairs(runs, ignore=(), defaults=None):
    # One masked signature per key: for key k, the run's values for every other
    # compared key. Two runs differ in exactly k when they share that signature and
    # their values for k differ; runs that also agree on k are identical configs.
    base = dict(defaults or {})
    skip = set(ignore)
    keys = set(base)
    for _, cfg in runs:
        keys.update(cfg)
    keys = sorted(k for k in keys if k not in skip)
    rows = []
    for run_id, cfg in runs:
        rows.append((run_id, tuple(cfg[k] if k in cfg else base[k] for k in keys)))   # never `or`
    out = []
    for i, key in enumerate(keys):
        groups = {}
        for run_id, values in rows:
            groups.setdefault(values[:i] + values[i + 1:], []).append((run_id, values[i]))
        for members in groups.values():
            if len(members) < 2:
                continue
            for a in range(len(members)):
                ra, va = members[a]
                for b in range(a + 1, len(members)):
                    rb, vb = members[b]
                    if va != vb:
                        out.append((ra, rb, key) if ra < rb else (rb, ra, key))
    out.sort()
    return out

Explanation. Two runs differ in exactly key k when they agree on every other compared key and disagree on k. So for each key k, take each run's values for every other key, in one fixed (sorted) key order: that tuple is the run's masked signature for k. Runs that share a masked signature agree everywhere except possibly at k; inside such a group, two runs with different values at k are an ablation pair on k, and two runs with the same value are identical configs, which are skipped. A pair that differs in one key appears in exactly one key's grouping, so no pair is reported twice. Normalising first matters: one effective tuple per run, in sorted key order, with defaults filled by key presence (cfg[k] if k in cfg else base[k]), never by truthiness, so an explicit 0.0, 0 or False stays a value, and with ignored keys dropped before any signature is built.

Complexity. O(n·k) dictionary operations on tuples of length k − 1, so O(n·k²) work to build the signatures, plus the size of each group squared, which the data keeps small: O(n·k² + output). The timing test (24 000 runs, ten hyperparameters with four values each, about 15 000 pairs) takes about 0.35 to 0.45 s in CPython, and generating it about 0.15 s. Comparing every pair took about 6 s at 4 000 runs; at 24 000 that is about 230 s, extrapolated, more than 500 times the reference.

The middle approach. The likely middle answer groups runs by the value of one key first and compares every pair inside each group key by key, plus a separate pass for pairs that differ only in that key. With four values for that key, each group holds about 6 000 runs, so it is still about n²/8 comparisons. Measured on the timing test it takes about 22 to 23 s (about 50 times the reference), well over the 8 s limit, whichever key is chosen, because every key has four values. Ask how big a group is before accepting it. Grouping by a whole-config hash first and then by masked signatures is the reference with an extra step and is fine. Building all k masked signatures as strings (for example json.dumps of the dict with one key removed and sort_keys=True) is also O(n·k²) and passes if the serialisation is canonical.

Dialect notes. In SQL, unpivot configs to (run_id, key, value), then for each key compute a masked signature with string_agg(key || '=' || value, ',' ORDER BY key) FILTER (WHERE key <> k) per run, and self-join on (k, signature) with a.run_id < b.run_id and different values; or self-join on equal values and keep pairs where count(*) = number of keys − 1, which is quadratic. In Spark, explode one row per (run, masked key) and group by (key, signature). Java and C++ need a canonical, hashable signature (an immutable list or a string built in key order). Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. One key apart versus two keys apart; identical configs (not a pair) that each pair with a one-change variant; three values of one key (three pairs); ids out of order in the input; a string value and a boolean value; a single run ([]). Hard adds runs that differ only in an ignored seed (identical) and several ignored keys with a pair that also differs in one of them. Very Hard adds an omitted key equal to an explicit default and an explicit 0.0 that is not the default 0.1.

Common mistakes. Reporting identical configs as pairs; reporting a pair once per key it differs in; comparing ignored keys; filling defaults with cfg.get(k) or default, which turns 0.0 into the default; serialising dicts without sorting keys; comparing ids numerically after stripping a prefix; forgetting that keys can be absent at Very Hard and raising KeyError.

Follow-up guidance. (1) For at most two differing keys, mask every pair of keys: k(k − 1)/2 signatures per run, 45 for ten keys, still linear in n; pairs found under several masks must be deduplicated, and the reported keys are those where the values differ. (2) Normalise numbers before comparing (for example round to a stated number of significant digits, or compare the config as written by the launcher rather than computed values) and record the rule, because over-normalising hides real differences. (3) Flatten to dotted paths; treat a list as one value (a tuple) unless the team decides each position is a hyperparameter; record the flattening rule with the sweep. (4) Keep the k signature maps; a new run is looked up in each one in O(k²), producing its new pairs, and is then added. Deletions remove it from each map.

def plan_deletions(checkpoints, policy, pins):
    """checkpoints: dicts {"run", "step", "metric"}, one per saved checkpoint.
    policy: {"keep_last", "keep_best", "metric_mode": "min" | "max", "every"}.
    pins: (run, step) pairs that an evaluation still points at.
    Return the (run, step) pairs to delete, sorted."""
    keep_last = policy["keep_last"]
    keep_best = policy["keep_best"]
    every = policy["every"]
    lower_is_better = policy["metric_mode"] == "min"                 # the policy says min or max

    by_run = {}
    for ck in checkpoints:
        by_run.setdefault(ck["run"], []).append(ck)

    keep = set()

    # 1. the most recent checkpoints of each run
    for run, cks in by_run.items():
        latest = sorted(cks, key=lambda ck: ck["step"], reverse=True)
        for ck in latest[:keep_last]:
            keep.add((run, ck["step"]))

    # 2. the best checkpoints of each run by its evaluation metric; ties to the earlier step
    for run, cks in by_run.items():
        if lower_is_better:
            ranked = sorted(cks, key=lambda ck: (ck["metric"], ck["step"]))
        else:
            ranked = sorted(cks, key=lambda ck: (-ck["metric"], ck["step"]))
        for ck in ranked[:keep_best]:
            keep.add((run, ck["step"]))

    # 3. every Nth step, as a sparse history of the run (step 0 included)
    for ck in checkpoints:
        if ck["step"] % every == 0:
            keep.add((ck["run"], ck["step"]))

    # 4. checkpoints that an evaluation still points at, matched by run and step
    pinned = set(pins)
    for ck in checkpoints:
        if (ck["run"], ck["step"]) in pinned:
            keep.add((ck["run"], ck["step"]))

    return sorted((ck["run"], ck["step"]) for ck in checkpoints
                  if (ck["run"], ck["step"]) not in keep)

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. The last k across all runs. latest sorts every checkpoint of every run by step and keeps the first keep_last, so a long run's high steps take every slot. Symptom: a team's short runs lose all their recent checkpoints on a night when a long run is in the same batch. Fix: sort and slice inside the per-run loop.
  2. The metric direction is never "min". lower_is_better = policy["metric_mode"] == "lower" compares with a value the policy never uses, so it is always False and every metric is ranked higher-is-better. Symptom: for a loss, the worst checkpoints are kept as "best". Fix: compare with "min".
  3. Step 0 left out of the every-Nth rule. if ck["step"] and … is false for step 0, whatever every is. Symptom: the starting checkpoint is deleted. Fix: test ck["step"] % every == 0 alone.
  4. Pins matched by step only. pinned_steps keeps the step and drops the run, so a pin protects that step in every run. Symptom: a pin on one run's checkpoint keeps the same step in all other runs, and storage is not freed. Fix: match (run, step) against a set of pairs.
  5. Ties broken by input order. The sort key is the metric alone; Python's sort is stable (with reverse=True too), so equal metrics keep their input order, which changes from night to night. Symptom: the checkpoint kept as best changes between runs of the planner. Fix: sort by (metric, step) for "min" and (-metric, step) for "max", with no reverse.

Each bug has its own check in which the others do not show: two runs with very different steps, keep_last = 2 and no other rule active (bug 1); one run with metric_mode "min", distinct metrics and no step 0 (bug 2); one run with step 0 and keep_best = 0 (bug 3); two runs with the same steps, keep_last = keep_best = 0 and a pin on one of them (bug 4); one run in "max" mode with two tied best metrics, the later step listed first (bug 5). The other checks (a checkpoint kept by two rules with keep_last larger than a run, a pin on a checkpoint already deleted, a tie in "min" mode, and every rule at once) also catch one or more of the bugs and stay as regression checks. Random samples can hit several bugs at once at Hard and Very Hard. At Medium they hold a single higher-is-better run with no pins, no step 0 and no ties, so they pass on the original code and the checks carry the signal, which is deliberate: the reported symptoms come from the cases the samples do not cover.

Explanation. A retention plan is a union of independent "keep" rules, each scoped to a run, followed by one subtraction. Every bug breaks either the scope of a rule (bugs 1 and 4: per run, and per checkpoint identity), its meaning (bug 2: direction; bug 3: step 0 is a multiple of every N), or its determinism (bug 5). Fixing them keeps the structure: group once by run, sort within each run, then match on (run, step).

Complexity. O(n log n) for the per-run sorts and O(n + p) for the every-Nth rule and the pins. The timing test (50 000 or 100 000 checkpoints across 1 000 or 2 000 runs, 5 000 pins) takes about 0.2 to 0.45 s in CPython, and generating it about 0.1 to 0.2 s. A fix for bug 4 that scans the pin list for every checkpoint (any(r == run and s == step for r, s in pins)) is O(n·p), 500 million comparisons at the test size, and fails the timing check; so does building each run's list with a filter over all checkpoints (O(n · runs)).

Dialect notes. In SQL: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY run ORDER BY step DESC) for the last k; ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY run ORDER BY metric ASC, step ASC) (or metric DESC, step ASC for "max") for the best n; step % every = 0; a join to the pins on both columns; deletions are the checkpoints where none holds. NULLS FIRST/LAST matters if a metric can be missing: PostgreSQL sorts NULLs last in ascending order, MySQL first. Spark's window functions behave the same as PostgreSQL's here. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Two runs of very different lengths; a "min" metric; step 0; the same step in two runs with one pinned; tied metrics in both directions; keep_last larger than a run; a checkpoint kept by two rules; a pin on a checkpoint that no longer exists (and on a run that does not exist); all rules at once across three runs.

Common mistakes. Fixing bug 2 by flipping reverse for both modes; fixing bug 5 with reverse=True on a (metric, step) key, which puts the later step first among ties; fixing bug 3 with step >= every; matching pins with a string f"{run}:{step}" without checking for separators in run names; rewriting the function instead of making minimal fixes.

(1) Plan only over checkpoints marked complete (a manifest written last, or a commit marker), and treat the newest complete checkpoint as the latest; never let an in-progress one count towards keep_last. (2) Return, or log alongside the plan, the rules that kept each checkpoint, behind a new function or an optional argument so existing callers keep their output. (3) Re-read the pins and re-check the plan immediately before each deletion (or take a lease on the pin table), and make deletion move files to a short-lived trash first, so a late pin can still restore them. (4) Record per checkpoint planned, deleting and deleted, delete shards idempotently, mark a checkpoint deleted only when every shard is gone, and resume deleting ones on the next run; never count a half-deleted checkpoint as kept.

Strong signals. Reads the policy's allowed values before reading the code; tests ties with the input in both orders. Red flags. "Ties do not matter, any best checkpoint is fine"; fixing the pin bug with a nested loop over the pins.

GDM-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Client library. Metric calls append to an in-memory buffer and return at once; a background thread sends batches every few seconds or at a size limit. The buffer is bounded; when it fills, the client spills to local disk, and when that fills it drops points by a stated policy (oldest first, or keep every Nth step) and counts what it dropped, so training never blocks. Each batch carries (run_id, attempt, client_seq); retries resend the same identity. Run metadata (config, seed, code version, environment) is sent once at start and is required before metric batches are accepted.
  • Write API. Stateless servers validate a batch (size, number of new metric names, step ranges), append it to a durable log partitioned by run_id, record (run_id, attempt, client_seq) in a batch ledger, and acknowledge. A batch already in the ledger is acknowledged without being applied again. Per-run and per-project quotas reject a runaway job with a clear error the client surfaces in the job's own logs.
  • Resumes. A resume calls start_attempt(run_id, from_step), which records attempt n+1 with the checkpoint step it resumed from. Points are stored keyed by (run_id, metric_id, step, attempt). The value shown at a step is the one from the highest attempt that wrote it; lower attempts' points above the resume step are marked superseded, not deleted, and remain queryable for debugging. Late points from an older attempt therefore never replace a newer attempt's values.
  • Storage. Run metadata in a relational store (runs, attempts, configs as immutable rows keyed by a content hash, checkpoints with step, path and status). Metric names are interned per project into ids. Points go to a time-series layout partitioned by run, clustered by (metric_id, step), with columnar files compacted from the log, so one run's series is one sequential read.
  • Comparisons. For every run and metric, a summary row (last value, best value and step, count, last step) and downsampled series at a few resolutions (for example 1 000 and 10 000 buckets by step), each bucket keeping first, last, min and max, so a spike survives. They are updated incrementally as points arrive and rebuilt for a run after a resume or late points. A comparison of {{compare_runs}} runs reads summaries plus one downsampled series per run.
  • Limits. Caps on metric names per run, points per run per minute and batch size, enforced at the API with explicit errors and visible in the run page; the cap that triggered is recorded with the run.

Competing designs to accept. Writing points straight to a time-series database with upserts on (run, metric, step) plus an attempt column; a stream processor maintaining downsampled series instead of batch compaction; storing only the latest attempt's values and archiving superseded points to cold storage. All are fine if retries are harmless, the latest attempt wins per step, superseded values survive, and comparisons read summaries rather than raw points.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Clients that block training on a slow tracker; last-write-wins by arrival, which lets late points from an old attempt win; metric-name explosions; hot partitions for a few huge runs; downsampling by averaging, which hides spikes; comparisons that scan raw points; configs edited after the run started.

Incident guidance.

  • Attempt 1's late points replaced attempt 2's values: the store kept the last value written for a step instead of the value of the latest attempt. Store points per attempt, resolve the shown value by attempt number, rebuild the affected run's summaries and downsampled series, and add a check that alerts when a point arrives for an attempt lower than the run's current one (and counts them).
  • A metric per parameter group, millions of names in an hour: there was no cap on metric names per run. Reject new names above a per-run cap with a clear error, quarantine the run's extra names, clean them from the shared names table, and give each project its own name space so one sweep cannot slow everyone else.
  • Write API down for forty minutes; some jobs dropped points, others stalled: clients had unbounded or blocking send paths. Make sends asynchronous with bounded memory plus disk spill, a stated drop policy with counts reported when the API returns, jittered backoff so the backlog drains without a stampede, and a health signal so the client switches to spill early.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The client spills to disk and drains with jittered backoff and a rate cap; the API prioritises fresh points over backlog per run, and the batch ledger makes replays harmless. (2) A per-run name cap at the API; the job sees an error in its own logs and the run page says which cap was hit; the names already written stay readable. (3) Read {{compare_runs}} summary rows and {{compare_runs}} downsampled series of about 1 000 buckets each; never raw points, which are read only when someone zooms into a range of one run. (4) Overlay the attempts on the run page with the resume step marked, and compute the difference between attempts over the overlapping steps; the config and code version of each attempt are shown side by side.

Rubric anchors. 2: the job writes synchronously to the tracker, or points are overwritten by arrival, or comparisons scan raw points. 3: async bounded client, idempotent batches, per-attempt storage with the latest attempt shown, summaries and downsampled series. 4: also min/max-preserving downsampling, quotas with clear feedback, immutable configs, and a plan for each incident.

Strong signals. Asks what a resume does to steps before designing storage; separates "the value shown" from "the values stored". Red flags. "The client retries until the tracker accepts it" with no bound; "average the points into buckets".

GDM-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Pinned snapshot and diff. The release starts from a numbered catalogue snapshot, copied into the pipeline's own store with its checksum. A diff against the previous release's snapshot, by accession and sequence checksum (and fragment for long sequences), classifies every entry: new, sequence changed, unchanged, withdrawn. A model-version change adds a fourth class, recomputed. The diff is a table kept with the release and drives every later step; its counts are part of the release notes.
  • Matching predictions. The prediction job hands over each prediction with the sequence checksum it was computed for and the model version. A prediction is attached to an entry only if its checksum equals the snapshot's checksum for that accession and fragment; anything else is rejected and listed. Carried-over entries are matched the same way, against the old prediction's recorded checksum.
  • Immutable files. Every file (structure in each format, confidence values, predicted aligned error) is stored under a name with entry id, model version and a content hash, write-once. A release is a manifest: entry → file names and checksums. Unchanged entries point at the files they already had, so nothing is copied; only {{changed_share}} of entries produce new files.
  • Validation gates. Hard gates: every published entry's checksum matches the snapshot; every file exists, parses, and has a checksum equal to the manifest's; per-organism completeness (entries expected from the diff equals entries present); counts reconciled with the diff; per-residue confidence arrays as long as the sequence. Warnings: large shifts in confidence distributions per organism, unusually many withdrawals. A release goes live only after the hard gates pass and a named person signs off; both are recorded.
  • Archives. Per-organism archives are built from the manifest; an archive whose set of entry files is unchanged since the last release is carried over by reference with its checksum. Each archive has a checksum file, and a release-wide manifest lists every archive and every file with checksums, so mirrors can verify and fetch only what changed.
  • Switch and rollback. The website, the API and the download index all resolve "the live release" from one small, versioned pointer (a row or an object) and nothing else. Going live is one write of that pointer after everything is published and validated; rolling back is the same write with the previous release id. Past releases stay in the immutable store; withdrawn entries keep their old versions.

Competing designs to accept. Rebuilding every file each release if the candidate measures the cost at {{entries}} entries and argues for simplicity; separate pointers per surface switched by one orchestrated transaction with a verification step; per-organism staged go-live. All are fine if a prediction can never be published under the wrong sequence, files are immutable, and no surface can show a different release from the others.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Matching by accession alone; rebuilding and re-uploading unchanged files and archives; mutable file names that change content; switches done surface by surface; a rollback that cannot find the previous files; archive checksums computed before the final bytes; gates that warn when they should fail.

Incident guidance.

  • Predictions published for accessions whose sequence had changed: the match compared accessions, not sequence checksums. Withdraw the affected entries from the latest release (a new pointer, not edited files), publish a correction notice listing them, recompute them, and make the sequence-checksum match a hard gate with a test that injects a changed sequence.
  • Every per-organism archive rebuilt every release: archives were built from scratch rather than from the manifest diff. Carry over archives whose content set is unchanged, rebuild only organisms with changes, deduplicate storage by content hash, and track per-release bytes written as a release metric with a budget.
  • The API moved and the website did not, for {{switch_minutes}} minutes: each surface had its own notion of the live release. Put all three behind one pointer, read per request (or cached with a short bound and the release id carried in every response), and add a post-switch check that samples entries through every surface and compares release ids and file checksums.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Rebasing means re-running the diff; only accessions whose checksum changed between the two snapshots need new predictions, so the cost is that subset's compute plus revalidation. Decide by the size of that subset and the release date, and record which snapshot the release is aligned to. (2) That organism fails its hard gate: either exclude the affected entries (and say so in the notes) or hold the organism's archive, while releasing the rest if completeness rules allow; never publish them. (3) Publish a release manifest with per-archive and per-file checksums and stable names; mirrors diff manifests to fetch changes and verify each file. (4) Publish the fix as new files under new versioned names in a point release; old files and their checksums stay as they were, so citations still resolve, and the release notes explain the change.

Rubric anchors. 2: accession-only matching, or files overwritten in place, or surfaces switched separately. 3: pinned snapshot and diff, checksum matching, hard gates, immutable files with carry-over, archives with checksums, one release pointer. 4: also reconciled counts and sign-off, archive carry-over, a rollback that is one pointer write, mirror-friendly manifests, and a plan for each incident.

Strong signals. Asks how a prediction proves which sequence it was computed for; treats the release as a manifest over immutable files. Red flags. "Copy the new release over the old one"; "switch the API first, then the website".

GDM-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Projects, experiments, runs. projects (project_id, name), experiments (experiment_id, project_id, name, created_at), runs (run_id, experiment_id, started_at, ended_at NULL, parent_run_id NULL, parent_checkpoint_id NULL, sweep_id NULL, resolved_config_hash, code_commit, code_diff_hash NULL, image_digest, data_snapshot_id, launched_by_role). Everything that defines the recipe is written once, when the run starts, and never updated. A run continued with a changed config is a new run with parent_run_id and parent_checkpoint_id (this exercise's rule).
  • Layers. config_layers (layer_hash PK, kind base|project|experiment|sweep|cli, canonical_json, created_at, source_hint), content-addressed: the hash of the canonical form (sorted keys, normalised numbers such as 3e-4 and 0.0003 to one representation, booleans and nulls normalised). run_layers (run_id, position, layer_hash) keeps the order. Editing a file creates a new layer; old runs still point at the old hash.
  • Resolved config with provenance. resolved_configs (resolved_config_hash PK, canonical_json) shared by runs with equal configs, plus run_config_keys (run_id, key_path, value_json, set_by_position) or, at {{config_keys}} keys per run, the same information as one compact provenance map per run (a key → position array stored next to the resolved JSON). Keys that queries filter on often (learning rate, batch size, model size) are promoted to typed columns or a secondary index.
  • Seeds and environment. run_seeds (run_id, purpose data_order|init|eval_sampling|other, seed); image digest, library lock-file hash, accelerator type and count recorded on the run.
  • Checkpoints. checkpoints (checkpoint_id, run_id, step, written_at, uri, bytes, checksum, retention_state kept|expired|deleted, deleted_at NULL); deleting a file updates the retention state through an event, never the row's identity.
  • Named recipes. named_recipes (recipe_id, project_id, name) and recipe_pointers (recipe_id, target_run_id or target_config_hash plus code/data pins, valid_from, valid_to NULL, recorded_at, superseded_at NULL): two time axes, so "pointed at on D, as recorded on D" filters recorded_at <= D and "as known now" ignores superseded rows.
  • Run metadata. run_metadata_events (run_id, field status|tag|note|invalid, value, reason, editor_role, recorded_at); the current view is the latest event per field, and any report can ask for the state as of its own date.
  • Queries. Exact recipe: run row + run_layers + resolved JSON + seeds + checkpoints. Attributed diff: full outer join of two runs' key maps on key_path, with each side's set_by_position mapped to the layer kind. Affected runs for a bad key in layer L: runs whose run_layers contain L and whose provenance says L set that key (a later layer did not override it).

Competing designs to accept. One JSONB resolved config per run plus a provenance JSON, with GIN or extracted columns for the common filters. Event-sourced runs (a run-created event carrying the full recipe). Storing only layers and resolving on read, if the resolver is versioned and pinned, and the candidate explains how a resolver change could alter old results (and caches the resolved form anyway). A recipe pointer modelled as SCD type 2 is fine at 3 if the second time axis is missing; at 4 the candidate keeps both.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Layers stored by file path (history lost); hashes over non-canonical JSON (equal configs, different hashes); a key-per-row table at {{config_keys}} keys × {{runs_per_week}} runs a week (billions of rows a year) with no compact alternative; a mutable status column; named recipes as a single current pointer; no record of uncommitted code changes; seeds recorded as one number when several random streams exist; checkpoints deleted with their rows, breaking lineage.

Incident guidance.

  • Re-rendered config does not match: layers were stored by path. Recover the original content from the run's own logged resolved config (if logged) or from version control at the run's commit, store it as a content-addressed layer, and repoint run_layers; make content-addressed storage of every layer a precondition for a run to start.
  • Weekly report rewrote last month: the join used the recipe's current target. Join each run to the pointer row in force at started_at (and recorded before the report's date for an as-recorded view); add a test that historical reports are stable when only the pointer moves.
  • Key-per-row table too large: keep the resolved JSON and a compact provenance map per run, extract the frequently filtered keys into columns, and compute diffs on the fly from two documents; drop or archive the key-per-row table.

Follow-up guidance. (1) As recorded on D: pointer rows with valid_from <= D < valid_to and recorded_at <= D_end, latest recorded_at wins; as known now: the same with superseded_at IS NULL. They differ when a pointer was corrected or back-dated after D. (2) Runs containing layer L whose provenance attributes that key to L; runs where a later layer set the key are listed apart as "used the layer, not the bad value". (3) Library versions and lock files, accelerator type and count, non-deterministic kernels, data loader worker count and shard order, the evaluation set version, environment variables, and hardware faults; say honestly that some non-determinism cannot be pinned. (4) Resolved JSON stored once per distinct hash, typed columns for hot keys, and a provenance map; estimate bytes per run.

Rubric anchors. 2: a config blob or file path per run, editable runs, one current recipe pointer. 3: content-addressed layers, resolved config per run, seeds, code and data recorded, checkpoints, recipe history. 4: also per-key provenance and attributed diffs, canonical hashing rules, bitemporal recipe pointers and metadata, affected-run queries that honour overrides, storage sized and incident repairs that keep history.

Strong signals. Asks how equal configs are recognised; separates "what the run used" from "what the name meant". Red flags. Recomputing old runs' configs from today's files; deleting invalid runs; treating one seed as enough.

GDM-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Definitions. sources (source_id, name, priority), source_versions (source_version_id, source_id, version_label, ingested_at, record_count, manifest_checksum); source names can change, ids cannot. licence_records (licence_record_id, source_version_id, permitted_uses, terms_ref, reviewer_role, valid_from, recorded_at, superseded_by NULL): reviewers' records, append-only, with a second time axis for corrections.
  • Passes. pass_definitions (pass_id, kind filter|quality|dedup|mix, version, params_json, params_hash). snapshots (snapshot_id, built_at, status building|ready|superseded|withdrawn, supersedes_snapshot_id NULL, recipe_hash), where the recipe hash covers input source versions, the licence records read, and the ordered pass definitions with parameters (a different threshold is a different snapshot). snapshot_inputs (snapshot_id, source_version_id, licence_record_id_read).
  • Pass runs and counts. pass_runs (pass_run_id, snapshot_id, position, pass_id, attempt, status, started_at, ended_at); pass_counts (pass_run_id, source_version_id, records_in, records_removed, records_out) written only for the attempt that succeeded (keyed by (snapshot_id, position, source_version_id) so a retry replaces, never appends). Cross-source deduplication adds dedup_pair_counts (pass_run_id, kept_source_version_id, removed_source_version_id, records): how many records of one source were removed because another source's copy was kept under the priority rule.
  • Manifest. shards (snapshot_id, shard_no, uri, bytes, checksum, record_count), shard_source_counts (snapshot_id, shard_no, source_version_id, records), and the withdrawal index record_shard_index (record_id, snapshot_id, shard_no) written with the manifest (opaque ids only, partitioned by snapshot, retained while any run that read the snapshot matters).
  • Consumption. run_reads (run_id, snapshot_id, shard_no, first_step, last_step) or ranges of shards per run segment; checkpoints link to runs, so affected checkpoints are those written after the first read of an affected shard.
  • Withdrawals. withdrawals (withdrawal_id, source_version_id, scope all|records, received_at), withdrawn_records (withdrawal_id, record_id). Impact: snapshots with that source version in snapshot_inputs (scope all) or with withdrawn record ids in record_shard_index; runs from run_reads on those shards; checkpoints by run and step.
  • Reconciliation. Per snapshot and source version: first pass records_in = source version count; for each consecutive pass, records_out = next pass's records_in; records_in = records_removed + records_out; final records_out = Σ shard_source_counts. A failing snapshot never becomes ready.

Competing designs to accept. A lineage graph store (datasets as nodes, passes as edges) if counts per source still reconcile. Per-record lineage in columnar files outside the database, queried only for withdrawals. Replacement builds that rerun only deduplication and later passes, starting from cached filter outputs per source version, as long as deduplication is recomputed across all remaining sources.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Matching by source name; contents or samples stored "for debugging"; retried passes appending counts; a single snapshot_id per run; mutable manifests; licence as a free-text column on the source; deduplication decisions reused after inputs change; the record index sized without thought ({{shards_per_snapshot}} shards × records per shard × {{snapshots_per_month}} snapshots a month).

Incident guidance.

  • Withdrawal matched by name: match on source_version_id; rebuild the impact list from snapshot_inputs and record_shard_index; tell the owners of the wrongly flagged runs; add a test that a renamed source keeps its id.
  • Counts recorded twice after a retry: make pass_counts keyed by the pass position and source version with the attempt that succeeded; delete the duplicate attempt's rows; block ready on reconciliation.
  • Replacement kept old dedup decisions: deduplication is a function of all its inputs. Rerun the deduplication pass on the remaining source versions (cached filter outputs make this cheaper), let copies previously removed in favour of withdrawn records return, and show it in dedup_pair_counts of the new snapshot.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The equations above as a query with a failure list; failing snapshots stay building with a reason, never silently fixed. (2) Impact via the index and run_reads; replacement = same recipe minus withdrawn records (or source version), filters reused per source version, deduplication and mix recomputed; the new snapshot supersedes the old one. (3) Under the priority rule the other copy becomes the kept one, so the other source's count rises; the new dedup_pair_counts show it. With {{dedup_scope}} the near-match variant also changes cluster membership, so recompute rather than patch. (4) Records per snapshot × bytes per (record id, shard) entry; partition by snapshot; keep while any dependent run or checkpoint is retained.

Rubric anchors. 2: a snapshot table with a path and a source list; no counts per pass; contents kept to answer questions. 3: source versions, licence records, pass runs with reconciling counts, immutable manifests, run-to-snapshot links. 4: also licence history with what each build read, cross-source deduplication counts and correct replacement builds, shard-grain consumption, the record-to-shard index sized, and incident repairs.

Strong signals. Writes the reconciliation equation unprompted; sees that withdrawing a kept copy changes other sources' counts. Red flags. Storing samples of content; deciding licence questions in the pipeline; editing a ready snapshot.

GDM-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Catalogue identity. catalogue_accessions (accession, organism_id), catalogue_sequences (accession, sequence_version, length, sequence_checksum, effective_on); residue numbers are 1-based positions in a given sequence version.
  • Entries. entries (entry_id, accession, fragment_no) (one per accession, or one per fragment), entry_versions (entry_id, entry_version, sequence_version, model_version, residue_start, residue_end, computed_at, mean_confidence, share_very_high, share_confident, share_low, share_very_low) (the bands are this exercise's), immutable once released. Fragment ranges follow {{fragment_rule}}, stored explicitly per fragment so the rule's version can change without rewriting history; fragment_rules (rule_version, threshold, length, step) referenced by the entry version.
  • Per-residue confidence. One array per entry version (confidence SMALLINT[] or a compact blob, or one columnar file per release partitioned by organism). At {{entries}} entries × about {{median_length}} residues that is {{entries}} × {{median_length}} values per release (up to about a hundred billion at the largest sizes): fine as arrays or columnar files, painful as rows. Summary columns serve filters.
  • Files. entry_files (entry_id, entry_version, kind coordinates_cif|coordinates_pdb|confidence_json|aligned_error_json, format_version, bytes, checksum, uri). The aligned-error file is about length² values ({{median_length}}² values for a median-length entry, about 90,000 to 200,000), so it is never a table.
  • Releases. releases (release_id, released_on, catalogue_snapshot, notes_ref), release_members (release_id, entry_id, entry_version, carried_over bool): carry-over is a membership row pointing at an older entry version, never a copy. release_archives (release_id, organism_id, uri, bytes, checksum, member_count) built only from release_members.
  • Queries. Citation "E, v" → entry_versions by key. Behind the catalogue → membership joined to the sequence version in force now (the GDM-L3-05 query). Residue i of A in R → members of R for A, fragments whose range contains i; choose by the overlap rule (max of min(i − start, end − i), ties to the lower fragment number); read element i − start + 1 of that fragment's array.

Competing designs to accept. Per-residue data only in files, with summary statistics in the database. A document store per entry version with arrays inside. Releases modelled as snapshots of a manifest table instead of membership rows, if old releases stay reproducible and archives are built from them.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Accession as the only key (sequence changes collide); fragment-local positions without offsets; residue rows at {{entries}} entries; recomputing summaries for carried-over entries; archives from "latest version" instead of membership; mutable entry rows that break citations; any column suggesting a biological or medical conclusion from confidence.

Incident guidance.

  • Archive mixed releases: rebuild the archive from release_members, publish it with a new checksum and a notice listing the change; add a check that every file in an archive is a member of its release.
  • Fragment offsets missing: store residue_start per fragment and map positions on read; republish affected files as a new entry version only if file contents change; add a test that every fragment's array length equals its range.
  • Summaries recomputed for carried entries: summaries belong to the entry version and are computed once; carry-over adds membership rows only, so release work scales with recomputed entries, not {{entries}}.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The residue query above, with the tie rule written out. (2) New entry_versions for the recomputed 10%; membership rows for all members (old versions for carried ones); archives rebuilt per organism from membership, including unchanged files. (3) A catalogue merge maps two accessions to one: the old entries stay citable under their versions; the next release has one entry for the surviving accession and an accession_redirects table for the retired one. (4) Values × bytes per value for confidence; Σ length² × bytes for aligned-error (dominant); both in object storage, with summaries in the database.

Rubric anchors. 2: one row per accession updated in place; residue rows; no release membership. 3: identity, entry versions, fragments, files with checksums, releases with membership. 4: also the overlap rule made answerable, compact per-residue storage sized, carry-over by reference, archives from membership, citations stable, and incident repairs.

Strong signals. Separates the catalogue's versioning from the database's; estimates the length² growth. Red flags. Overwriting entries; storing aligned-error matrices as rows; drawing medical meaning from confidence.

GDM-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Reference data. detector_versions (detector_version_id, content_type, released_at, retired_at NULL, withdrawn_at NULL, outcome_definitions_ref, confidence_thresholds_ref); file_outcome_rules (rule_version, definition) (this exercise's rule: part = at least one segment detected and at least one not detected).
  • Checks. checks (check_id, received_at, channel api|web|partner, requester_category, content_type, format, size_bucket, duration_bucket NULL, file_key NULL, detector_version_id). file_key is a keyed hash (HMAC with a rotating secret) kept for this exercise's window and stored only in the operational table; analytics tables never carry it. No identifiers beyond the category reach analytics.
  • Results. segment_results (check_id, segment_no, unit ms|token|region, start_pos, end_pos, outcome detected|not_detected|uncertain, confidence_level high|medium|low); file_results (check_id, outcome all|part|none|inconclusive, confidence_level, rule_version, derived_at).
  • Repeated checks. Reports count checks, and count files by file_key with the latest check in the window; after the window the key is dropped and files cannot be linked, which is stated in the report.
  • Rollouts. During a rollout the service may run both versions on a sampled share of checks: paired_results (check_id, version_a, outcome_a, level_a, version_b, outcome_b, level_b), no content needed because both results come from one check.
  • Aggregates. agg_daily (day, content_type, detector_version_id, outcome, confidence_level, requester_category, checks, files) built from detail after late results have arrived (or rebuilt when they arrive), then suppression: cells under {{min_cell}} are withheld, and complementary cells are withheld too where a published total would reveal them. Suppression is a separate final step with its own version, so a rebuild reapplies it.
  • Retention. Segment detail kept for a short window; file results longer; aggregates indefinitely. At {{checks_per_day}} checks a day the segment table dominates, so it is partitioned by day and content type.

Competing designs to accept. Aggregates kept as a cube with suppression applied at read time (only if every reader goes through it). Differential privacy noise on published counts instead of (or alongside) suppression, if the candidate explains the trade-off. Not linking repeated checks at all, if the report says it counts checks, not files.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Storing content or thumbnails for debugging; unkeyed hashes that let anyone with the file find its check; requester ids in analytics; mixing versions in one series; suppression before late data or without complementary cells; raw scores compared across versions with different definitions; unbounded segment tables at {{checks_per_day}} checks a day. Any discussion of how detection works or how a watermark could be weakened is out of scope; steer back.

Incident guidance.

  • "Part" share jumped during the rollout: version the file-outcome rule with the detector version, report per version (never one mixed series), and annotate the rollout; check the old rule against the new version's segment shapes before ramping.
  • A small cell was published: rebuild the week's aggregates after late data and reapply suppression with complementary cells; retract the published table; make publishing depend on the final suppression step having run after the last merge.
  • Segment growth slowed the daily job: partition detail by day, aggregate incrementally from the day's partition only, and shorten segment retention; the aggregate job never reads a month of detail.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Any detected and any not detected → part; all detected → all; none detected and none uncertain → none; otherwise inconclusive (or the candidate's stated variant, recorded as a rule version). (2) Paired results from one check, as above; agreement per content type and confidence level, with versions' different definitions acknowledged. (3) Differencing published totals; complementary suppression or publishing totals only at coarser grains. (4) Detail partitioned by day with short retention for segments; aggregates kept.
